name: Abitub
title: Benjamite descendant, son of Shaharajim
summary: Abitub appears in the Benjaminite genealogies in 1 Chronicles as the son of Shaharajim and Husim, and brother of Elpaal. He is known exclusively from this genealogical material, with no independent narrative attached to his person. Genealogical lists like this serve an important theological and social function in the Chronicler's work: they confirm the tribes' identity and continuity in an unbroken line from the patriarchs. Abitub's presence in the overview testifies to the careful preservation of Benjaminite family history – a matter that gained renewed relevance in connection with the people's restoration after the exile, when questions of familial belonging and inheritance rights were of decisive importance.

footnotes.text: The name Abitub (Hebrew: אֲבִיטוּב, 'Avituv) means 'my father is goodness' or 'father of goodness'. It is composed of 'av' (father) and 'tuv' (goodness), a common pattern in Hebrew naming where 'father' is used metaphorically to denote the origin or source of a quality.

According to 1 Chronicles 8:8, Shaharaim sent away his wives Hushim and Baara and later had children with other wives in Moab. The fact that Abitub and Elpaal are still called sons of Hushim (verse 11) may suggest that these were born before the separation, or that the text preserves an older genealogical tradition with a different perspective on family relationships.

The tribe of Benjamin played a central role in Israel's history. The tribe gave Israel its first king, Saul, and remained attached to the kingdom of Judah after the division of the realm. The detailed genealogies in 1 Chronicles 8 served an important function in documenting the tribe's identity and continuity, especially after the return from the Babylonian exile.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles were recorded after the exile but contain material spanning many generations. Shaharaim's connection to Moab (1 Chron 8:8) suggests migration or connections between Benjaminite families and Moabite territory, reflecting the complex demographic reality of ancient Israel.
